sections.title: Intraoperative Red Flags: The 'Big Three'
content: Sudden deepening of the AC (Posterior Capsule Rupture)
Hard eye + Loss of red reflex (Expulsive Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage)
Asymmetric 'Argentinian Flag' sign (Intumescent tear risk)
Loss of followability or vitreous in the port

sections.title: Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR) Management
content: Step 1: Freeze! Do not pull the phaco tip out; maintain AC stability with OVD through the sideport.
Step 2: Inject dispersive OVD beneath the nuclear fragments to prevent posterior migration.
Step 3: Lower bottle height/aspiration settings and remove phaco tip carefully.
Step 4: Perform Bimanual Anterior Vitrectomy (cut/suck mode) using high cut rate (2500+ CPM).
Step 5: Assess residual capsular support; implant IOL in sulcus with optic capture or ACIOL if needed.

sections.title: The Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study (EVS) Protocol
content: Visual Acuity 'Light Perception' (LP) only: Immediate PPV is indicated.
Visual Acuity 'Hand Motion' (HM) or better: Tap & Inject is sufficient.
Antibiotics: Vancomycin (1mg/0.1ml) + Ceftazidime (2.25mg/0.1ml).
Amikacin is an alternative for Ceftazidime but carries risk of macular toxicity.

content.explanation: R: Retained fragment; A: Acute Endophthalmitis; P: Pressure (IOP) spike; I: Iritis/TASS; D: Detachment of Retina.

branches: First-line: Topical NSAIDs (Nepafenac 0.3% or Bromfenac) + Steroids
Second-line: Sub-tenon Triamcinolone or Intravitreal Anti-VEGF
Risk Factors: Diabetes, ERM, Vein Occlusions, Prostaglandin use

sections.title: UGH Syndrome (Uveitis-Glaucoma-Hyphema)
content: Etiology: Mechanical chafing of the iris/ciliary body by IOL (often ACIOL or sulcus IOL).
Signs: Micro-hyphema, pigment dispersion, elevated IOP, chronic low-grade inflammation.
Management: Topical IOP lowering and steroids; often requires IOL exchange or repositioning.
High-yield: Use Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM) to visualize IOL-haptic-iris contact.

sections.title: Late Complication: PCO
sections.content: Posterior Capsule Opacification (PCO) is the most common late complication. It results from the migration and proliferation of residual lens epithelial cells (LECs). Types include Fibrotic (metaplastic LECs) and Elschnig Pearls (swollen LECs). Management is YAG Laser Capsulotomy. Note: Perform only after 3 months post-op to allow IOL stability and prevent CME risk.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: ESCRS Antibiotic Prophylaxis
content: Study showed a 5-fold decrease in endophthalmitis with intracameral Cefuroxime (1mg in 0.1ml).
Current Trends: Use of intracameral Moxifloxacin (Vigamox off-label) is increasing in the US.
Povidone-iodine (5%) in the conjunctival sac for 3 minutes is the single most important aseptic step.

sections.title: Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage Management
content: 1. Immediate recognition: AC shallows, IOP rises, loss of red reflex.
2. Rapid wound closure: Use 10-0 Nylon immediately to secure the eye.
3. Stop the surgery: Do not attempt to drain blood in the primary setting.
4. Post-op: Systemic steroids and IOP control. Delayed drainage (7-14 days) if choroidals are kissing.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Nearly 100% PCO rate: Primary Posterior Capsulotomy + Anterior Vitrectomy (PPC+AV) is mandatory.
Higher inflammatory response: Require aggressive topical/systemic steroids.
Risk of Glaucoma: Lifetime risk of 'Aphakic Glaucoma' even after successful IOL placement.

rows: Poor dilation (use Malyugin rings), phacodonesis assessment.
Zonular dialysis; use Capsular Tension Ring (CTR) or CTS.
Late IOL-Capsular bag complex dislocation (Sunset Syndrome).
High risk of post-op IOP spikes and corneal decompensation.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: The 'Seidel Test' should be performed on every clear corneal wound if a leak is suspected.
Don't chase a dropped nucleus: If a large fragment goes south, perform vitrectomy and refer to a vitreoretinal surgeon.
Descemet's Detachment: Usually occurs at the incision; inject air or 20% SF6 to 're-bubble' the membrane.
IOL Power Error: Rule out wrong biometry or transcription error before considering IOL exchange or piggyback IOL.

sections.title: --- Sub-topics from: Post-Cataract Surgery Complications: The Master Clinical Roadmap ---
sections.content: An exhaustive guide to identifying and managing post-cataract surgical complications, ranging from posterior capsule rupture to endophthalmitis. This poster integrates incidence statistics, intraoperative management protocols, and clinical pearls for the anterior segment surgeon.

sections.title: Signs of Posterior Capsule Rupture (PCR)
content: Sudden deepening or shallowing of the Anterior Chamber (AC)
Momentary pupillary dilation
Nucleus falls away and cannot be approached by phaco tip
Marked slowing of aspiration due to clogged vitreous in phaco tip
Torn capsule may be directly visible
Vitreous gel may be directly visible

sections.title: Sequelae of Vitreous Loss after PCR
PCR Management: Core Principles
content: Management depends on the magnitude of the tear
Depends on the size and type of any residual lens material
Depends on the presence or absence of vitreous prolapse
CRITICAL: Do NOT pull out the phaco probe immediately (maintains AC pressure)

sections.title: PCR Surgical Protocol
content: Step 1: Inject dispersive viscoelastic before removing phaco probe
Step 2: If a complete or nearly complete nucleus remains, convert to ECCE
Step 3: If residual nuclear fragments, remove by phaco using low bottle height and low aspiration flow rate
Step 4: If large fragments, use visco-expression after extending the main wound
Step 5: Once remnants are removed, replug the tear with dispersive OVD
Step 6: Gently fill the AC with cohesive viscoelastic
Step 7: Use manual aspiration cannula with irrigation OFF to aspirate residual cortex
Step 8: Remove all vitreous from AC, wound, and capsular tear with a vitrector
Step 9: Infusion cannula of vitrector remains HIGH; Cutter remains LOW
Step 10: Visualize vitreous using 0.1 ml of 40mg/ml Triamcinolone

rows: Constrict pupil following PC IOL or prior to AC IOL

sections.title: Clinical Complications: Continuous List
sections.content: Additional complications noted include: Corneal decompensation, chronic endophthalmitis, and specific post-operative inflammation rates ranging from 2% to 6%. PCO remains a primary late complication at 10% within 2 years.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Acute Post-Op Vision Loss

rows: Immediate onset (12-24h), no pain, limbus-to-limbus edema
Elevated IOP, corneal edema, mid-dilated pupil
Loss of red reflex, sudden pain, AC shallowing

sections.title: CRITICAL RED FLAGS
content: Endophthalmitis (0.1%): Immediate referral if pain/hypopyon present
Choroidal Haemorrhage (0.1%): Intraoperative disaster requiring immediate wound closure
Loss of nuclear fragment posteriorly (0.3%): Requires vitreoretinal consultation
Wound leak (1%): Risk for hypotony and endophthalmitis
Iris Prolapse (0.7%): Requires surgical repair to prevent infection

content.explanation: D: Deepening/shallowing of AC. R: Red reflex change/loss. O: Out of reach nucleus (falls away). P: Pupil dilation (momentary).

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: Vitreous Visualization
content: Always use preservative-free Triamcinolone (0.1ml of 40mg/ml) to stain vitreous strands.
Stained vitreous appears as white specks trapped in the gel, making clean-up far more precise.
Ensure AC is stable with OVD before starting the vitrectomy cutter.
